name: Xiongnu Confederation

areaKm2.note: The world_bc200 Xiongnu polygon measures 3.24 million km2 on the sphere (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aourednik/historical-basemaps/master/geojson/world_bc200.geojson, mid); Seshat codes 4.0-4.2 million for 209 BCE (high); Seshat Late Xiongnu low is 3.0 million.

population.note: Seshat codes 1,500,000 for the Xiongnu Imperial Confederation (209 BCE) and 1.0-1.5M for the Late Xiongnu; its narrative says the nomads north of China did not number more than 1,500,000 (Barfield 1993). Mid 1.2M for 200 BCE, early in Modu's reign.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Largest settlement 3,000-5,000 (Seshat 272); practically no towns.

activePersonnel.note: Population 1.2M (Seshat 272) x ~1 warrior per 8 people = 150,000. Bounds from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Baideng: the Book of Han claims over 300,000 Xiongnu at Baideng (200 BCE) and Shiji credits Modu with 300,000 bowmen; Chang 2007 p. 158 says 400,000; Gumilev argues 20,000-40,000 on pasture and population grounds. With ~1.2M people the whole confederation could field ~150,000-250,000; mid 150,000 standing. audit 2026-10-30: date basis: the snapshot is dated to the Baideng campaign (winter 200 BCE), when Modu had his host assembled in the field, so the muster counts as active (as zulu-kingdom-1879 counts the January 1879 assembly); in a year without a campaign most of it would be trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Remaining adult males of subject tribes (Donghu, Yuezhi remnants) callable within a month.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Herders moving remount herds, smiths, Chinese defectors and craftsmen.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Nomadic adult males were all mounted archers; one warrior per four to six people is the usual steppe ratio.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess. Horse archers, nearly the whole army; ~90% of the active total.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75 (among the era best). Evidence: composite bows, several remounts each

training.note: Rubric row: training 1.0 (elite long-service). Evidence: lifelong riders and hunters; Modu's whistling-arrow discipline

count.note: Educated guess. Armoured noble retinues; the elite of the chanyu's guard.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: some iron and leather armour, lighter than Han lancers

training.note: Rubric row: training 1.0. Evidence: same lifelong training

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.75-1.0. Evidence: Modu trapped the Han emperor at Baideng and destroyed the Donghu and Yuezhi

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5-0.75. Evidence: decimal command under the chanyu, but a confederation of clans (left and right kings)

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75 (recent victories). Evidence: victories over Donghu, Yuezhi and Han in 209-200 BCE

weapons.note: Anchor: between 2 (composite bow) and 3. Evidence: composite bow, bronze and iron arrowheads, swords

armor.note: Anchor: about 2. Evidence: leather and some iron plates; most riders unarmoured

ships.note: Anchor: 0 (rafts). Evidence: no boats beyond river crossings

fortification.note: Anchor: between 1 and 2. Evidence: few walled sites; Ivolga-type fortresses are later

logistics.note: Anchor: 3 (equivalent reach). Evidence: self-moving herds gave long reach on grassland

communications.note: Anchor: between 2 (couriers) and 3. Evidence: mounted messengers, whistling-arrow signals

isr.note: Anchor: 3. Evidence: deep mounted scouting, Chinese defectors as informants

gdpPerCapita.note: Educated guess. Pastoral economy plus tribute and raiding; below the agrarian Maddison band (~950-1,100) for neighbours.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. A pastoral society in which every adult man was a soldier; no budget.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Some iron working and crafts; pastoral economy.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Herds plus some agriculture by captives and subject peoples; tribute grain from Han under heqin.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots.

majorPorts.note: Landlocked steppe polity; analogue Mongol Empire 1241 (no ports).

merchantTonnage.note: No merchant marine; analogue Mongol Empire 1241.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Herds and remounts let armies roam far on pasture (analogue to the Mongols).

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Horses, sheep-borne camps, camels and oxen; Mongolia carries ~4M horses today.

homeDefense.note: 1.3 row: deep steppe and harsh continental climate; the 119 BCE Han expedition lost most of its 140,000 horses.

notes: Snapshot 200 BCE, the year of Baideng, eight years into Modu Chanyu's reign. All army figures are Chinese claims (Shiji, Book of Han: 300,000+); the mid follows the population ceiling (Seshat, Barfield). Population convention: the nomadic confederation inside the bc200 polygon; subject oasis states of the Western Regions (from ~176 BCE) are not counted. Production is empty: no documented figures. Personnel: active = the warriors of the chanyu's decimal units (every adult nomad man, a household force always under arms); trainedReserves = men of subject tribes; mobilizable = population x ratio.
